title: March Madness, Leadership, and the Energy You Bring Into the Room
content:
**You learn more about leadership from how someone handles a loss than a win.**

March Madness is one of the purest examples of emotional volatility—high stakes, no control, and instant outcomes. As a UCLA fan, I watched my team lose this past Sunday. Like anyone invested, I felt the frustration.

But over time, I’ve become more intentional about one thing:

**How I process that emotion—and more importantly, how much of it I allow to affect others.**

---

## An Early Lesson That Stuck

Growing up, one of my good friend’s dads was a die-hard USC fan.

You didn’t want to be around on Saturdays when they lost.

The shift in energy was immediate. The house felt different. Conversations changed. You learned quickly that something external—a game—could dictate the tone for everyone around him.

That stuck with me.

Because even as a kid, it was clear:
**His reaction didn’t just belong to him. It impacted everyone in the room.**

---

## The Spillover Effect

As leaders—at work and at home—we carry something that’s easy to underestimate:

**Emotional spillover.**

* A bad loss
* A missed target
* A broken release
* A decision that didn’t go your way

Individually, these are part of the game. But unmanaged, they bleed into everything else:

* How we speak to our teams
* How we show up at home
* How people experience us

And the reality is:

**People don’t separate your context—they experience your presence.**

---

## Passion Is Not the Problem

I love sports. I care deeply about the teams I follow. That passion is part of what makes life enjoyable.

But passion without discipline becomes volatility.

And volatility—especially from someone in a leadership role—creates uncertainty for everyone else.

The goal isn’t to care less.
It’s to **contain the impact of what we care about.**

---

## The Standard: Emotional Discipline

One of the most important—and least talked about—leadership skills is **emotional discipline**.

Not the absence of emotion.
Not suppressing frustration.

But the ability to:

* Recognize it
* Process it
* And choose how (and where) it shows up

Because every interaction is shaped by the energy you bring into it.

You are either:

* Creating clarity and stability
* Or introducing tension and unpredictability

---

## Creating Separation

The best leaders build separation between:

* What happens *to* them
* And how they show up *for* others

That might look like:

* Taking a beat before your next meeting
* Channeling frustration into a workout
* Resetting before walking through your front door
* Being aware enough to say, “I’m off today—let me recalibrate”

These aren’t signs of weakness.

They’re signs of control.

---

## The Real Win

I’ll keep watching UCLA. I’ll keep caring. I’ll keep feeling the highs and lows that come with it.

But I’m more mindful now of what actually matters:

**The people around me should not pay the price for outcomes they had no part in.**

Not from a game.
Not from a bad day at work.
Not from anything external I don’t control.

Because at the end of the day, leadership isn’t just about decisions or results.

It’s about consistency of presence.

---

## Final Thought

**Be the person people can rely on—not the one they have to read the room for.**

That’s true in sports.
That’s true in business.
And that’s true at home.

The scoreboard will always fluctuate.

**Your impact on others shouldn’t.**

title: NIL, Accountability, and the Missing Middle in College Athletics
content:
March Madness always brings big moments—but sometimes the headlines off the court are the ones worth paying attention to.

A recent suspension of a top Alabama men’s basketball player for off-court issues raises a bigger question that goes beyond one athlete or one program:

What does accountability look like in the NIL era?

Over the last few years, NIL has fundamentally changed college athletics.

We now have:
• Athletes earning six- and seven-figure deals
• High school recruits entering college with multi-million dollar valuations
• Transfer portal movement driven by market dynamics, not just playing time

In many ways, this looks a lot more like a professional ecosystem than anything college sports has ever seen.

But here’s the disconnect:
👉 We are compensating athletes like professionals
👉 Without building the systems that typically come with professional environments

In any company:
• Compensation comes with clear expectations
• Contracts include behavior and performance clauses
• There are defined consequences tied to risk and brand impact

That structure is what makes the system sustainable.

In college athletics today, that structure is still fragmented.

NIL collectives, universities, sponsors, and governing bodies are all operating in parallel—but not always aligned. That creates inconsistency in how accountability is applied.

At the same time, there’s another reality we can’t ignore:

These are still 18–22 year olds.

They are:
• Managing sudden access to money
• Operating as personal brands
• Navigating visibility and pressure most adults haven’t experienced

And they’re doing it without the infrastructure that usually surrounds high earners.

So the answer isn’t simply “treat them like pros” or “protect them like students.”

We need a middle ground.

A more complete model would include:

1. Professional-level accountability
Clear, standardized expectations tied to NIL agreements—with real consequences when those expectations aren’t met.

2. Institutional support systems
Financial literacy, legal guidance, and mentorship should be built into the experience—not optional add-ons.

3. Development-focused intervention
When issues happen, the response shouldn’t just be punitive. It should include a path for growth, correction, and reintegration.

Because ultimately, this isn’t just about protecting programs or brands.

It’s about building people.

Right now, NIL has accelerated the “compensation” side of college athletics.

The next step is maturing the structure around it.

If we get that right, we don’t just produce better athletes—we produce better leaders, teammates, and professionals.

And that’s a win that lasts longer than any tournament run.

title: Navigating the Storm: Geopolitics, Oil, and Raising a Child in 2026
content:
The world feels particularly volatile these days. As global tensions escalate, we're seeing profound impacts on the economic landscape. The ongoing geopolitical conflicts in the Middle East, particularly the situation involving Iran, have severely disrupted the flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz—a critical chokepoint for global oil supplies.

The resulting economic shockwaves are undeniable. Crude prices have surged, with forecasts warning of further increases if disruptions persist. For the average person, this doesn't just mean more expensive gas at the pump; it signals a broader, creeping inflation that risks stalling global economic growth and straining everyday budgets. Supply chains are tightening, and the cost of essential goods is climbing.

But reading these headlines as an economist or a market analyst is fundamentally different from reading them as a father.

When you're trying to raise a young child in the midst of this macroscopic uncertainty, the focus shifts dramatically. The abstract numbers on a screen—the percentages of GDP growth, the barrel prices, the inflation indices—suddenly translate into very real anxieties about the future. Will the world be stable enough for them to thrive? How do we balance preparing for economic downturns with providing a sense of security and joy at home?

The tension between the macro and the micro is a daily balancing act. You read an analyst's report warning of energy shocks, and then you sit on the floor building blocks, trying to foster resilience and optimism in a little person who has no idea what a barrel of crude oil is.

Raising a child requires a profound, relentless hope. It demands that we look past the immediate geopolitical storms and invest in the long term. Much like navigating volatile markets, parenting requires patience, adaptability, and an unwavering commitment to the future. It’s a stark reminder that while the geopolitical maneuvers in distant straits impact our wallets, the most significant investments we make are in the resilience and well-being of the next generation.

title: Immigration: The Under-Appreciated Economic Stabilizer
content:
Long-term immigration is one of the most under-appreciated economic stabilizers in the U.S.

Government and non-partisan research show that many long-term immigrants—especially those without full paperwork—contribute financially while under-utilizing public benefits. Undocumented immigrants alone pay an estimated $90–100B per year in federal, state, and local taxes, including tens of billions into Social Security and Medicare, programs they are largely ineligible to access (ITIN and payroll withholding data).

At the same time, they disproportionately work low-paying but essential jobs—construction, agriculture, hospitality, caregiving—that keep businesses operating and help suppress inflationary pressure on goods and services. The National Academies of Sciences has shown that immigrant labor lowers prices across multiple sectors by expanding labor supply where shortages are most acute.

Like most economies throughout history, the U.S. has always had a shadow labor market. While imperfect, it has acted as a pressure valve—supporting output, moderating prices, and absorbing demographic and demand shocks.

The biggest payoff is intergenerational. Immigrants invest heavily in their children’s education and mobility. Long-run analyses cited by the Congressional Budget Office show that immigration expands the labor force, increases GDP, and improves fiscal outlooks over time as second-generation Americans become higher-earning, fully tax-paying contributors.

In short: immigration isn’t a short-term cost—it’s a deferred economic investment with compounding returns.

title: Harnessing AI for Strategic Growth: Lessons from Recent Partnerships
content:
# Harnessing AI for Strategic Growth: Lessons from Recent Partnerships

In a rapidly evolving market, the integration of **artificial intelligence** (AI) into core business operations is not just a trend—it's becoming essential for competitive survival. The recent partnership between **SAP** and **Syngenta** illustrates this shift, as they commit to embedding AI into Syngenta’s global operations to enhance productivity and innovation.

This development highlights a key observation: **AI is no longer an optional add-on; it’s a necessity for businesses aiming to modernize and scale.** As industries like agriculture embrace AI to optimize their processes, other sectors must take note. The synergy of technology and product management is becoming a pivotal driver of market success.

For product leaders, the strategic takeaway is clear: **invest in AI capabilities** that can enhance your product offerings and streamline operations. In a landscape where competition is fierce, adopting AI can not only improve efficiency but also foster innovation that meets evolving consumer demands. As we look to the future, the companies that prioritize AI will likely lead the charge in their respective markets, shaping trends rather than following them. Embrace this change and position your products at the forefront of this technological revolution.
